title: Rubin and the Rift
caption: The Great Rift above Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Cerro Pachón
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site
credit: NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/H. Stockebrand

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Above NSF NOIRLab's Vera C. Rubin Observatory on Cerro Pachón, the Great Rift seems to divide the Milky Way. The dark band is made of a chain of cold dust clouds where stars are actively forming. The clouds are so dense that they block the light of the stars behind them, and that blocking creates the rift.

The U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy fund Rubin jointly. At the time of this release it was due to start science operations in late 2025. Once complete, it was to use an 8.4-meter mirror and the largest astronomical camera ever built for a decade-long survey called the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), imaging the whole southern sky every 3–4 nights.

One planned goal was to catch transients, objects whose brightness or position changes quickly, such as supernovae, variable stars and asteroids. Transients can reveal processes that shape the Universe, and frequent observations like Rubin's are expected to push astronomy forward in ways no one can yet predict.

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by Hernán Stockebrand. No camera or exposure details or color mapping are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the night sky would look fainter to someone standing at the site.
